subject: Biology
title: Molecular Mechanism of Muscle Contraction: Sliding Filament Model
learningObjectives: Trace excitation-contraction coupling from motor end plate ACh to sarcoplasmic Ca2+ release
Diagram the 6 stages of the cross-bridge power stroke cycle
Identify which sarcomere bands shorten vs remain constant during contraction
Explain the molecular etiology of Rigor Mortis
content:
Proposed by H.E. Huxley & A.F. Huxley (1954), the **Sliding Filament Theory** states that muscle contraction occurs when thin actin filaments slide inward over thick myosin filaments toward the M-line, pulling Z-discs closer together.

```
                     NEUROMUSCULAR EXCITATION CASCADE
                     
   Motor Neuron Action Potential ──► Reaches Neuromuscular Junction (Motor End Plate)
                                                 │
   Exocytosis of Acetylcholine (ACh) ◄───────────┘
               │
   Binds Nicotinic ACh Receptors on Sarcolemma ──► Generates Muscle Action Potential
                                                              │
   Depolarization spreads down T-Tubules ─────────────────────┘
               │
   Opens Ryanodine Receptors (RyR1) on Sarcoplasmic Reticulum
               │
   Massive Release of Ca²⁺ Ions into Sarcoplasm
```

### 4.1 Stepwise Cross-Bridge Power Stroke Cycle

```
                         CROSS-BRIDGE POWER STROKE CYCLE
                         
   1. Ca²⁺ binds Troponin-C ──► Tropomyosin shifts ──► Unmasks Myosin-binding sites on Actin.
   2. Myosin ATPase hydrolyzes ATP (ATP → ADP + Pᵢ) ──► Myosin Head "Cocked".
   3. High-energy Myosin Head binds Actin ──► Forms CROSS-BRIDGE.
   4. POWER STROKE: Release of Pᵢ & ADP causes Myosin head to pivot, pulling Actin inward.
   5. Fresh ATP binds Myosin Head ──► Detaches Cross-Bridge from Actin.
   6. ATP hydrolyzed ──► Myosin re-cocked for next cycle.
```

### 4.2 Structural Dimensional Changes during Contraction

```
                   STRUCTURAL CHANGES DURING CONTRACTION
                   
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ SHORTER / NARROWED                       │ REMAINS CONSTANT                         │
   ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 1. Sarcomere Length (Z-lines closer)     │ 1. A-Band Length (Myosin length)         │
   │ 2. I-Band Length (Actin overlaps)        │ 2. Actin Filament Length                 │
   │ 3. H-Zone (Disappears completely)        │                                          │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Rigor Mortis**: Following somatic death, cellular ATP synthesis stops completely. Without fresh ATP binding, cross-bridges cannot detach from actin filaments, causing permanent, rigid post-mortem muscle stiffness until lysosomal autolytic enzymes degrade myofilaments ($12\text{--}24\text{ hours}$).

conceptBreakdown.heading: The ATP Paradox in Muscle Physiology
conceptBreakdown.explanation: ATP plays two opposing but essential roles: (1) Hydrolysis of ATP is required to energize (cock) the myosin head to initiate contraction, and (2) Binding of fresh unhydrolyzed ATP is required to break the actin-myosin bond to allow relaxation.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Role of Dihydropyridine & Ryanodine Receptors
conceptBreakdown.explanation: T-tubule depolarization activates voltage-sensing Dihydropyridine Receptors (DHPR / Cav1.1), which are mechanically coupled to Ryanodine Receptors (RyR1) in the SR membrane, instantly releasing stored Ca2+.
